etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English licence, licens, lisence, lissens, licance, from Old French licence, from Latin licentia (“license”), from licens, present participle of licere (“to be allowed, be allowable”); compare linquere, Ancient Greek λείπω (leípō, “leave”).

definitions.definition: A legal document giving official permission to do something; a permit.

quote.citation: 1970, 0:1:15 from the start, in Monty Python's Flying Circus, season 2, episode 10, John Cleese (actor):
quote.text: Hello. I would like to buy a fish licence please.

definitions.definition: The legal terms under which a person is allowed to use a product, especially software.

quote.citation: 1986, Thomas Smedinghoff, The Legal Guide to Developing, Protecting, and Marketing Software‎[1], page 166:
quote.text: Thus, while the license will grant the user the right to use the software, a major concern is the scope of that use. For example, will the user be granted the right to copy, modify, or transfer the software?

definitions.definition: Freedom to deviate deliberately from normally applicable rules or practices (especially in behaviour or speech).

quote.citation: 2012, Chris Seepe, The Conspiracy to Assassinate Jesus Christ‎[2], page 5:
quote.text: In some instances, the author took license to include events which never happened, or to purposely create events which may run in the face of popular conjecture if the author felt it would help the story along.

definitions.definition: Excessive freedom; lack of due restraint.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto XXVII, page 44:
quote.text: I envy not the beast that takes⁠His license in the field of time,⁠Unfetter’d by the sense of crime,To whom a conscience never wakes;  […]

quote.citation: 1936, Will Durant, Ariel Durant, The Story of Civilization, page 520:
quote.text: When liberty becomes license dictatorship is near.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English licencen, licensen, lisensen, licent, from Old French licencer, licencier, licenciier, licenser, from Medieval Latin licentiō (cf. English licentiate).

definitions.definition: To give formal authorization to use.

quote.citation: 2013 June 22, “T time”, in The Economist, volume 407, number 8841, page 68:
quote.text: The ability to shift profits to low-tax countries by locating intellectual property in them, which is then licensed to related businesses in high-tax countries, is often assumed to be the preserve of high-tech companies.

definitions.definition: To acquire authorization to use, usually in exchange for compensation.

quote.citation: 2000, International Journal of Micrographics & Optical Technology‎[3]:
quote.text: As part of the strategic relationship, Microsoft has licensed the image segmentation, compression and viewing technology from ScanSoft.

quote.citation: 2007, Steve Swayne, How Sondheim Found His Sound‎[4]:
quote.text: They changed their campaign, licensed the song and used it for over six years in all of their advertising.

definitions.definition: (transitive) (applied to a piece of intellectual property)
(transitive) To give permission or freedom to; accept.

quote.citation: 1855 December – 1857 June, Charles Dickens, Little Dorrit, London: Bradbury and Evans, […], published 1857, →OCLC:
quote.text: Intruders there were in Harley Street, of whom it was not aware; but Mr and Mrs Merdle it delighted to honour. Society was aware of Mr and Mrs Merdle. Society had said ‘Let us license them; let us know them.’

quote.citation: 2014, Hagit Borer, Parametric Syntax: Case Studies in Semitic and Romance Languages‎[5]:
quote.text: Kayne argues that the crucial fact which licenses preposition stranding in English but not in French is the fact that in English verbs and prepositions assign Case similarly, and hence they govern similarly.
